chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ali ibn al-Nu'man from Sa'id al-A'raj said:
I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the fasting person who tastes something but does not swallow it, so he said, 'No.'

Because this narration is understood to refer to one who has no need for that, and the concession was only mentioned for the mother of the infant or the cook who fears the spoilage of his food, or one who has a bird that will perish if he does not feed it. As for one who is independent of all that, it is not permissible for him to taste with food.

key_terms.يَزُقَّهُ: he feeds it (by putting food in its beak)

ai.seo_question: Does tasting food break the fast if not swallowed?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that tasting food without swallowing does not break the fast, but this ruling is context-dependent, applying primarily to those with a specific need such as a mother tasting for her child or a cook preventing spoilage. For the individual who is self-sufficient and lacks such necessity, the concession does not apply, rendering it impermissible to maintain the spirit of fasting. This distinction highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle of linking legal rulings to the underlying wisdom (hikmah) and practical necessity rather than applying them uniformly.
